Yes, it is possible. Here is the construction and proof.

## Construction

Let $\{q_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be any enumeration of the rational numbers in $[0,1]$, i.e., $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1] = \{q_1, q_2, q_3, \dots\}$, with each rational appearing exactly once. Set $x_n := q_n$.

## Proof

We verify the three required properties.

**Claim 1: $\liminf_{n\to\infty} x_n = 0$.**

For every $n$, the tail $\{q_k : k \ge n\}$ is a cofinite subset of $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$, hence is dense in $[0,1]$. In particular, $\inf_{k\ge n} x_k = 0$ for every $n$ (there are rationals in $(0, \varepsilon)$ appearing at indices $\ge n$). Therefore
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty} x_n = \lim_{n\to\infty}\Big(\inf_{k\ge n} x_k\Big) = \lim_{n\to\infty} 0 = 0.$$

**Claim 2: $\limsup_{n\to\infty} x_n = 1$.**

By the same density argument, $\sup_{k\ge n} x_k = 1$ for every $n$ (rationals in $(1-\varepsilon, 1]$ appear at arbitrarily large indices). Hence
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} x_n = \lim_{n\to\infty}\Big(\sup_{k\ge n} x_k\Big) = \lim_{n\to\infty} 1 = 1.$$

**Claim 3: For every $\alpha \in [0,1]$, there is a subsequence of $\{x_n\}$ converging to $\alpha$.**

Fix $\alpha \in [0,1]$. Since $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ is dense in $[0,1]$, for each $m \ge 1$ there exists a rational $r^{(m)} \in \mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ with $|r^{(m)} - \alpha| < 1/m$ and $r^{(m)} \in [\max(0,\alpha-1/m),\, \min(1,\alpha+1/m)] \subseteq [0,1]$. Each $r^{(m)}$ equals $q_{n_m}$ for a unique index $n_m$.

We extract a subsequence with strictly increasing indices. Set $n_1$ to be the index of $r^{(1)}$. Having chosen $n_1 < n_2 < \dots < n_{m-1}$, choose $r^{(m)}$ (and hence $n_m$) with $n_m > n_{m-1}$: this is always possible because among the infinitely many rationals within $1/m$ of $\alpha$, only finitely many can have index $\le n_{m-1}$, so at least one has index $> n_{m-1}$.

Then $\{x_{n_m}\} = \{q_{n_m}\} = \{r^{(m)}\}$ satisfies $|x_{n_m} - \alpha| < 1/m \to 0$, so $x_{n_m} \to \alpha$.

## Conclusion

The sequence $x_n = q_n$, an enumeration of $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$, satisfies $\liminf x_n = 0$, $\limsup x_n = 1$, and has a subsequence converging to every $\alpha \in [0,1]$. Therefore such a sequence exists.

### PROOF COMPLETE
